items.title: Bourdieu's forms of capital
items.claim: Pierre Bourdieu argued that economic, cultural and social capital interact to reproduce class. What did he mean by 'cultural capital'?

options.text: Embodied dispositions, qualifications, and familiarity with high-status culture

items.reveal_title: Knowledge, manners and credentials function as inheritable assets
items.reveal:
Bourdieu (1986) distinguished embodied (dispositions), objectified (cultural goods) and institutionalised (qualifications) forms.

Empirical work continues to show cultural-capital indicators predict educational outcomes net of income.
items.why: Cultural capital explains why income alone underestimates the inheritance of advantage.

items.title: Disadvantage gap in England
items.claim: England's 'disadvantage gap' tracks attainment of pupils eligible for free school meals against peers. After narrowing in the 2010s, what happened from 2019?

options.text: It widened, including after pandemic disruption
It reversed: FSM pupils overtook peers

items.reveal:
Education Policy Institute analyses reported the disadvantage gap at GCSE widened from 2019, reaching its widest in over a decade by 2022.

Pandemic-related school closures appear to have amplified pre-existing trends.
items.why: Apparent progress can reverse when systems are stressed, revealing structural fragility.

items.title: The Chicago School's method
items.claim: Robert Park and the Chicago School in the 1920s pioneered which approach to studying social life?

options.text: Urban ethnography, mapping the city as a social laboratory

items.reveal_title: The city itself as a research site
items.reveal:
Park urged students to study the 'gold coast and the slum' through direct observation. The result included Wirth's Ghetto (1928), Anderson's The Hobo (1923) and Whyte's Street Corner Society (1943).

The school established urban sociology as a recognised field.
items.why: Method choice shapes what counts as evidence and what kind of theory is possible.
